narrationPlan.voice: One clear, warm narrator throughout; no character voices
narrationPlan.pace: Clear, warm, and measured (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a single narrator: this is a science article, not a story with characters.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Say numbers and units in full ("one hundred and fifty million kilometres", "astronomical units") and pronounce names clearly.

music: Soft xylophone (gyil) pattern with light drum (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Curriculum link: JHS Social Studies B9.4.5.3.1, Strand 4: Law and Order, Sub-Strand 5: Promoting Democracy and Political Stability (Assess the significance of political stability in national development).
Original article written for Ghanaian JHS learners from widely known history and oral tradition. It is not copied from any book.

Local accuracy: the Wa Naa’s palace stands in central Wa; the Nakore mosque is a few kilometres away. The three estates of Wala society are the princes (Nabihi), the Muslims (Yerihi), and the landowners (Tendaamba). Chieftaincy succession in Wa has been disputed; the article keeps to the general principle.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated JHS age band (Basic 7 to Basic 9) and BECE conceptual level?
Are all facts, figures, and dates accurate and up to date at the time of publication?
Ask the Wala Traditional Council or a historian to confirm the origin of the princes, which traditions give as Mamprugu or Dagbon.
Confirm the account of the Dumba ceremony with a Wala reviewer.

teacherGuide.overview: Shows how three groups with different origins formed one kingdom at Wa, and draws a lesson about unity in diversity.
learningGoals: Name the three groups of Wala society and what each contributed.
Describe Wa as a centre of Islamic learning.
Outline the events of the 1890s at Wa.
Explain how sharing roles holds a diverse community together.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics (NaCCA CCP: number and time; codes to verify)

beforeReading: Ask: can people of different origins and beliefs build one community? What makes it work?
whileReading: After Page 3, learners fill a three-column table: group, where they came from, what they gave.
afterReading: Learners design a badge for a club that shows three different groups working together.
discussion: Which was most important to the kingdom: the horse, the book, or the land? Can one work without the others?
reflection: Which different groups make up your own town, and what does each bring?

mathsExtension.task: Ferguson signed the treaty in 1894 and was killed in 1897. How many years later was that?
If four gates take turns to provide the king and each reign lasts 15 years, how long is one full round?

support: Give three learners a toy horse, a book, and a hoe, and let the class say what each stands for.
stretch: Find out who Samori Toure was and why he fought the French.

factCheck.explanation: The three estates of Wala society, the arrival of princes and Muslim scholars (dates uncertain), the rotating gates, Ferguson’s treaty (1894) and death (1897), and British control from 1898 come from general historical knowledge and should be confirmed by a historian. The Social Studies code was checked against the NaCCA CCP Social Studies curriculum document (NaCCA, 2021); the choice of strand for this article is the writer’s judgement.
